claims.text: The initial refractory high-entropy alloy is homogeneous and has minimal pre-existing microstructural heterogeneity.
Controlled high-temperature annealing promotes coherent nanoscale microstructural features.
Annealing-assisted elemental diffusion produces nanoscale short-range ordering, grain-boundary segregation, or nanoprecipitates.
The annealing-induced nanoscale features impede dislocation motion.
The annealing-induced nanoscale features alter phonon scattering or phonon interactions.
Impeded dislocation motion enhances the alloy's mechanical strength.
Altered phonon interactions modify the alloy's thermoelastic constants.
Annealed alloys will have higher yield strength than untreated, single-phase baseline alloys.
Annealed alloys will have greater creep resistance than untreated, single-phase baseline alloys.
Annealing will alter elastic modulus or thermal-expansion behavior relative to the untreated baseline.
Rapid quenching retains a single-phase microstructure with few thermal-treatment-induced features.
The proposed effect is significant only at high temperatures where diffusional processes are active.
The proposed effect applies to alloys that remain single-phase overall.
Changes in alloy composition or grain size outside the tested range may alter the observed behavior.
The intended service and test regime is above approximately 1000 degrees Celsius under mechanical load in an inert or vacuum environment.
Failure to observe statistically significant mechanical improvement, thermoelastic alteration, and clear microstructural differences in annealed samples would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: Nanoprecipitate formation generally implies a distinct precipitate phase, creating tension with the boundary condition that the treated alloy remain single-phase overall. Short-range ordering or segregation could satisfy that boundary, but the nanoprecipitate alternative may not.
